parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
Two parallel plate capacitors $C_1$ and $C_2$ are connected to a supply that has a potential difference (p.d.) $V_S$. The capacitors may be connected in series or in parallel.

The supply provides charge $Q_S$ and the plates of the two capacitors acquire charges $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ respectively. The p.d.s across the plates of the capacitors are $V_1$ and $V_2$ respectively.

Complete Table 6.1 to indicate how $Q_S$, $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ relate to each other, and how $V_S$, $V_1$ and $V_2$ relate to each other, for series and parallel connections of the capacitors to the supply.

Table 6.1

|  | relationship between charges | relationship between p.d.s |
| series |  |  |
| parallel |  |  |
hints: Hint 1: Picture the wiring - in series there is only one path for current, in parallel there are two separate branches across the same supply terminals.
Hint 2: For series, think about what must be the same on each plate because any charge that arrives on one capacitor must have come through the other.
Hint 3: For parallel, think about what is directly connected together - both top plates to one supply terminal and both bottom plates to the other.
Hint 4: Remember Kirchhoff ideas - p.d.s add round a loop in series, but charge splits at a junction in parallel.
parts.proper_answer: Series: $Q_S = Q_1 = Q_2$ and $V_S = V_1 + V_2$. Parallel: $Q_S = Q_1 + Q_2$ and $V_S = V_1 = V_2$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Think charge flow in series**
In series the same charging current flows through both capacitors. No charge is lost, so each capacitor ends up with the same magnitude of charge as was delivered by the supply. That gives $$Q_S = Q_1 = Q_2$$

Step 2: **Think p.d. in series**
The supply p.d. is shared between the two gaps. Going round the loop, the sum of the capacitor p.d.s must equal the supply p.d. So $$V_S = V_1 + V_2$$

Step 3: **Think p.d. in parallel**
In parallel both capacitors are connected directly across the supply. Each one feels the full supply p.d. So $$V_S = V_1 = V_2$$

Step 4: **Think charge in parallel**
The total charge from the supply splits at the junction into the two branches. Charge is conserved, so $$Q_S = Q_1 + Q_2$$

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem: An isolated capacitor of capacitance $470\,\mu\text{F}$ stores $19\,\text{mJ}$ of energy.
parts.text: Calculate the p.d. across the capacitor.
hints: Hint 1: You know the stored energy $19\text{ mJ}$ and the capacitance $470\,\mu\text{F}$ and you need the p.d. - focus on which energy relationship links just $E$, $C$ and $V$.
Hint 2: Convert mJ to J and $\mu\text{F}$ to F first, then rearrange to make $V$ the subject before substituting numbers.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Choose the right energy form**
You have $E$ and $C$ and want $V$, so use the form with those three: $$E = \frac{1}{2}CV^2$$

Step 2: **Rearrange and calculate**
Make $V$ the subject: $$V = \sqrt{\frac{2E}{C}}$$ Convert: $E = 19\times 10^{-3}\text{ J}$, $C = 470\times 10^{-6}\text{ F}$. Then $$V = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 19\times 10^{-3}}{470\times 10^{-6}}} = 9.0\text{ V}$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the charge on the capacitor.
hints: Hint 1: You now know $C$ and the p.d. you just found - think how charge, capacitance and p.d. are linked for a single capacitor.
Hint 2: Use your $9.0\text{ V}$ value with $C$ in farads to get $Q$ in coulombs, checking the power of ten carefully.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Q to C and V**
Capacitance is defined as charge per unit p.d.: $$C = \frac{Q}{V}$$ so $$Q = CV$$

Step 2: **Substitute values**
$$Q = (470\times 10^{-6}) \times 9.0$$ $$Q = 4.2\times 10^{-3}\text{ C}$$ This is the same as using $Q = \sqrt{2EC}$.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text:
The capacitor is now connected in parallel with a capacitor of capacitance $180\,\mu\text{F}$ that is initially uncharged.

Determine the total energy, in $\text{mJ}$, now stored in the two capacitors.
hints: Hint 1: The first capacitor is isolated then joined to an uncharged one - think about what total quantity cannot escape and must be shared between the two.
Hint 2: Think about how to combine the two capacitances when they are in parallel to get the new effective capacitance.
Hint 3: With the shared total charge and the new total capacitance known, think which energy formula uses $Q$ and $C$ to find the final stored energy.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Total charge is conserved**
The system is isolated, so no charge is lost when the second capacitor is connected. All the charge from (b)(ii) is now shared: $$Q_{total} = 4.23\times 10^{-3}\text{ C}$$

Step 2: **New total capacitance in parallel**
In parallel capacitances add: $$C_{total} = C_1 + C_2 = (470 + 180)\times 10^{-6}$$ $$C_{total} = 650\times 10^{-6}\text{ F}$$

Step 3: **Final stored energy**
Use energy in terms of $Q$ and $C$: $$E = \frac{Q^2}{2C_{total}}$$ $$E = \frac{(4.23\times 10^{-3})^2}{2 \times 650\times 10^{-6}} \approx 1.4\times 10^{-2}\text{ J} = 14\text{ mJ}$$ Notice energy is less than $19\text{ mJ}$ - some is lost as heat and in moving charge.
